newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CHANGES PLANNED TO S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTS.
newsitem.headline: CHANGES PLANNED TO S.AFRICAN GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTS.

text.p: South Africa's budget reform programme has taken another step forward with the decision by Auditor-General Henri Kleuver to change the format of government accounts.

Kleuver told members of the parliamentary public accounts committee on Wednesday that his annual report had become bigger every year because he wanted to be less cryptic than he had been in the past, while the audits had been more thorough.
This year it was a bulky 600 page document that was cumbersome to carry around and find information in.
"We said to ourselves that this was information overload and it is really not serving the purpose," he said.
So instead of one composite report, he planned to produce separate reports on the 36 government departments and entities audited on a first in, first out basis.
Once all the accounts had been completed a summary would be published as part of a smaller general report. There would be a separate report on revenue.
This would happen in 1996/97 and 1997/98 but thereafter departments would have to publish their own accounts, which would include the audit report.
"This is standard practice in parts of the business community and in some democratic countries," he said.

The Department of State Expenditure had said this would fit in with the model it was considering for government financial administration and which was contained in the draft white paper on budget reform.

The advantages of the new system would include the fact that the accounts would be published sooner, there would be a more manageable spread of information, the impact would be more effective and balanced and there would be better media coverage.
He said the departments would now have two years to prepare themselves to handle their own accounts instead of relying mainly on his staff to complete them.
He hoped that the new system would generate competition between government departments as to how quickly they could submit their accounts.
"If they are at the end of this chain, they could draw fire from the public accounts committee," he said.
Some committee members were concerned that separate reports would mean that they would "lose the big picture and the ability to identify trends".
Kleuver said this would be reflected in the general report.

He had specifically called the meeting to get the go-ahead to inform government departments about the envisaged changes, even though parliament had not yet elected a new public accounts committee under the new constitution.

This has been delayed because of legal uncertainties, but frustrated members of the former joint standing committee on public accounts planned to persuade parliament later on Wednesday to approve the establishment of a National Assembly committee on pulic accounts.

It used to be a joint standing committee representing both the National Assembly and Senate under the old constitution, but there has been uncertainty about whether this arrangement should be continued under the new constitution which has seen the Senate replaced by the National Council of Provinces.
